title: ASIRT clears officers in fatal shooting of David McQueen
article: Actions taken by Calgary police in a 2016 armed standoff that ended with the fatal shooting an emotionally disturbed gunman were both justified and reasonable, Alberta's police watchdog said Thursday.

This comes at the conclusion of the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) investigation into the Jan. 24, 2016 shooting death of 53-year-old David McQueen - one that ASIRT executive director Susan Hughson says was one of the more harrowing inquiries ever carried out by her office.

"Without the actions taken by CPS, combined with sheer good luck, the potential for a civilian or police officer to be seriously injured or killed would have been extremely high," she said during Thursday morning's press conference.
It was a little before 5 p.m. when reports of gunshots came from McQueen's home on 78th Ave. in Huntington Hills.
Bullets whizzed by the heads of officers attempting to contain the scene, slamming into neighbouring homes.
A nearby Calgary Transit bus was also struck, the bullet coming within centimetres of hitting the driver.
McQueen continued to open fire out both the front and rear of his home for the next 90 minutes, firing at least 30 shots from a handgun ASIRT says he wasn't legally allowed to possess.
The standoff came to an end when the CPS tactical unit launched tear gas canisters into the home in response to a fresh volley of gunfire from inside.
Hughson said this forced McQueen to emerge from the home and open fire on police.
"In response, two officers located to the southwest of the rear of the residence fired rounds from their C8 carbine rifles," she said.
They were joined by a tactical officer stationed on the roof of a nearby garage who fired three rounds from his .308 tactical rifle, fatally striking McQueen in the head.
That officer, whom sources tell Postmedia was a senior member of the tactical unit for over 10 years, is no longer employed by Calgary police.

He was one of two tactical officers who resigned earlier this year in response to service's controversial tenure policy that imposes mandatory limits on how long constables can work in speciality units before they're rotated back to patrol.
Nobody else was injured, and McQueen was the only person in the home at the time.

Confined to a wheelchair after a 1994 diving accident at Sikome Lake, reports described McQueen - originally from Windsor, Ont. - as a man struggling with mounting health issues, compounded by depression and increasing frustrations with the government and healthcare system.
Hughson commended the actions of both patrol officers and the CPS tactical team, clearing police of criminal wrongdoing in the incident.

"Notwithstanding his disability, the evidence demonstrates that not only was the man capable of using a firearm, he was capable of targeting officers and areas where officers were sheltered," she said.
She praised officers for exercising restraint in the face of McQueen's gunfire, saying the decision by scene commanders to enact a proactive tactical response "was more than reasonable."
Shots continued to come from both the front and rear of the home as police contained the scene and urged adjacent residents to seek shelter in their basements.
Armed with a handgun, McQueen emerged from the rear of the home just before 6 p.m. and directly confronted members of the CPS tactical unit.
Police opened fire, and McQueen was shot and killed.
Nobody else was injured, and McQueen was the only person in the home at the time.

Reports in the wake of the shooting described McQueen - confined to a wheelchair after a 1994 diving accident at Sikome Lake left him paralyzed - as a man struggling with mounting health issues, compounded by depression and increasing frustrations with both the government and Alberta's healthcare system.
In a statement issued Thursday afternoon, Calgary police said ASIRT's decision reaffirms the "reasonable and necessary" actions undertaken by officers that day.
"Facing high-risk dynamics, all steps were taken to contain the situation, eventually leading to few tactical alternatives," the statement read.
"The grief being endured by the family is not lost on the members of the Calgary Police Service. In our duty to protect public safety, we always strive for a resolution that preserves life."
